clue.text: Only bit I can translate — "peers"

indicators.note: to translate is to render into another form, so these letters are to be put into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone struggling with a foreign text can only manage one word, "peers".
explanation.walkthrough: 'can translate' rearranges ONLYBITI.
explanation.definitionFit: Peers of the realm collectively make up the aristocracy, the titled class.

clue.text: Hooter in front part of vehicle

definitions.meaning: hooter is British slang for the facial feature you smell with
the foremost projecting part of a car or plane

explanation.definitionFit: Slang for the facial feature, and also the projecting front end of a car or aircraft.

clue.text: Spent recklessly —- depressingly, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the word for depressingly is heard, then spelt differently

parts.note: blue means sad or depressing

explanation.surface: Someone splashed out wildly, which sounds rather gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: BLUE (sad) is said aloud to give BLEW.
explanation.definitionFit: To blow money is slang for squandering it, so blew means spent recklessly.

clue.text: Not an Italian wine, it gets spilt in ambush

indicators.note: spilling scatters things, so the remaining letters are jumbled
not an tells us to remove the letters an from the word Italian

explanation.surface: A glass of non-Italian wine is knocked over during a surprise attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not an' removes AN from ITALIAN to leave ITALI; 'it gets spilt' rearranges ITALI with WINE.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie in wait is to hide ready to attack, which is what an ambush means as a verb.

clue.text: Very fiercely sound horn to pass on corner

parts.note: to toot is to sound a horn
to hand is to pass something on
to nail someone is to corner or catch them

explanation.surface: An angry driver honks the horn to overtake on a bend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Fighting tooth and nail means with every possible effort, very fiercely.

clue.text: Stuck in cat-flap, do grannies notice pet?

indicators.note: the answer is stuck inside the run of letters cat-flap, do grannies

explanation.surface: Elderly ladies are asked whether they spotted a pet wedged in the cat-flap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuck in' signals letters running across catfLAP DO Grannies; 'notice' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A small pampered dog kept as a companion is a classic pet.

clue.text: Deck-there's trouble with sailors here

parts.note: ado is fuss or trouble
RN is the Royal Navy, sailors collectively

explanation.surface: Trouble breaks out on a ship's deck among the crew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck' looks like a ship's floor but is the verb to decorate.
explanation.definitionFit: To deck is to decorate or embellish, a direct verb synonym.

clue.text: First drink's imbibed in a state

indicators.note: imbibed means taken in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a draught is a drink or swallow
1st, spelt IST, is the abbreviation for first

explanation.surface: Someone's first drink is downed in an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'imbibed' is the container signal; 'in a state' looks like a place, but it is the idiom for being very upset.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a state is idiom for being very upset and anxious.

clue.text: Become entangled and express disapproval thus

definitions.meaning: literally to end up tied in knots
the phrase is a British dismissive retort, like telling someone to go away

explanation.definitionFit: Literally to become tangled, and also a rude British phrase of contemptuous dismissal.

clue.text: Observe places where grouse gather, turning over bones

indicators.note: turning the whole assembled run over means reading it from end to start

parts.note: to observe is to note
leks are the display grounds where grouse and similar birds gather to court

explanation.surface: A naturalist watches grouse gathering grounds while handling some bones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning over' reverses NOTELEKS as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A skeleton is the full framework of bones in a body.

clue.text: South-west area sorted out

indicators.note: sorted out suggests the letters are rearranged, out of their original order

explanation.surface: Something in the West Country has been put in order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges SORTED. DORSET is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorset is an English county on the south-west coast, so a south-west region.

clue.text: Luck begins to run out for intellectual

indicators.note: run out suggests the letters break out of their order into a new one

explanation.surface: Someone's good fortune starts to fail for a thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run out' rearranges LUCKBEGINSTO.
explanation.definitionFit: A bluestocking is a scholarly, intellectual woman.

clue.text: Eventually participating in marathon

definitions.meaning: eventually means ultimately, after a long time
literally, taking part in a long-distance race

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means ultimately, and read literally it describes a runner in a long race.

clue.text: Goes down hard in pothole —- a nasty moment

indicators.note: in places the losing-and-hard pieces inside the pothole word

parts.note: a pothole is a cave
loses, as a team goes down to defeat
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A caver slips down into a pothole and has a frightening moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes down' means loses, not descends.
explanation.definitionFit: A close shave is a narrow escape from danger, a nasty moment.

clue.text: Possibly links Head of Geography to radio lectures

parts.note: the head of Geography is G, which in the radio phonetic alphabet is said as Golf
a series of lectures is a course

explanation.surface: A head of department sends geography lectures out over the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: Radio operators use the NATO alphabet, in which G is Golf. 'Links' is a seaside golf course; 'Possibly' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Links are a kind of seaside golf ground, so the answer is an example of such.

clue.text: Lot of old fibre adapted initially as bathing accessory

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of each of the preceding five words

explanation.surface: A bath sponge is made from a lot of old fibre that has been adapted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' picks the opening letters of Lot of old fibre adapted.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofah is the dried fibrous gourd used as a scrubbing sponge in the bath.

clue.text: Swill dustmen see mostly — it's inevitable

indicators.note: to swill is to slosh around, so these letters are churned into a new order
mostly means the word see loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Refuse collectors are told to look at slops, which is unavoidable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts SEE to SE; 'Swill' rearranges DUSTMEN with SE.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb 'needs must' means one has to do what circumstances force, so it is unavoidable.

clue.text: I had dressed in a shawl, by the way — most dull

indicators.note: dressed in means wearing, so one piece sits inside the shawl

parts.note: a stole is a shawl
ID is the contraction for I had
ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Someone wearing a shawl is, by the way, the dullest person present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is a link joining ST.
explanation.definitionFit: Stolid means impassive and unexcitable, so the superlative is the dullest.

clue.text: Peter, beside river, takes time to get insurance

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
the Tyne is a river in north-east England

explanation.surface: A man called Peter sits by a river and takes his time arranging insurance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter' looks like a name but is thieves' slang for a safe; 'beside' and 'takes' place the pieces in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A safety net is a fallback protection against loss, a form of insurance.

clue.text: Old church, partly red —- yellowish-red

indicators.note: partly means only part of the word red is used, losing its last letter

explanation.surface: An old church is described as somewhat red, really a reddish yellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly' trims RED to RE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is an earthy pigment ranging from pale yellow to brownish red.

clue.text: With small racetrack, use more direct but irregular route

definitions.meaning: literally, possessing a little racing track

definitions.text: use more direct but irregular route
definitions.meaning: to bypass the proper channels by taking a shortcut

explanation.definitionFit: Read literally the phrase is a little track; as a verb it means bypass normal procedure.

clue.text: Brick to take trick

definitions.meaning: a brick is a reliable, good-hearted person
in card games, to beat a card by playing the master suit

explanation.definitionFit: Old slang for a splendid fellow, and the card play that wins a trick with the master suit.

clue.text: American writer — this principally defines him

definitions.text: American writer — this principally defines him

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe was an American writer

indicators.note: principally takes the first letter of the word this

explanation.surface: An American author is summed up by a single word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'principally' gives T from this; Poe plus T describes what Poe was.
explanation.definitionFit: Poe wrote verse such as The Raven, so a versifier is what defines him.

clue.text: Old artist loses his footing and goes over

indicators.note: goes over means the remaining letters are flipped upward
his footing is the bottom letter of his name in a down clue, which is dropped

parts.note: Degas was a French painter

explanation.surface: An elderly painter slips and falls over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses his footing' drops the S from DEGAS; 'goes over' turns DEGA upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Aged is a straightforward synonym for old.

clue.text: Ace, winning 50% in court, …

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for ace in cards

indicators.note: 50% keeps half of the word for winning, its first five of ten letters

parts.note: winning means triumphant

explanation.surface: A tennis ace takes a player halfway to victory on court.
explanation.walkthrough: '50%' keeps TRIUM, half of TRIUMPHANT; 'in' is a link. The ellipsis joins this clue to the next only for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An atrium is an open central court or hall in a building.

clue.text: … left one criminal heading for gaol, with no possibility of release

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a felon is a criminal

indicators.note: heading for takes the first letter of the word gaol

explanation.surface: A crook heading for prison gets a sentence with no chance of parole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading for' gives G from gaol (British spelling of jail).
explanation.definitionFit: A lifelong sentence lasts the whole of a life, so there is never any release.

clue.text: River police finally accept excuse

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon
MP stands for military police

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of the word accept

explanation.surface: Police by a river finally accept someone's excuse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' gives T from accept. The Exe is a river in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: To exempt someone is to excuse them from a duty, a verb synonym.

clue.text: A contemptible character, a youthful delinquent, is 7

parts.note: git is British slang for a contemptible person
a Ted, short for Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth often seen as a delinquent

explanation.surface: A lout and a young hooligan are described as being in a state.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cross-reference to 7 down, whose answer means frantic with worry.
explanation.definitionFit: The 7-down answer means frantically upset, which is close to being worked up and nervous.
